title: Thermal radiation and color
target: Use peak wavelength as one piece of evidence about a thermal spectrum.
criteria: Relate higher temperature to shorter peak wavelength.
Distinguish spectral peak from perceived color.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A thermal emitter’s absolute temperature triples. What happens to its peak wavelength in Wien’s law?
cpa.guide: λ_peak T is constant, so peak wavelength varies inversely with kelvin temperature.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Emitter A peaks at 1.2 micrometers and B at 0.6 micrometers. For ideal thermal emitters, which is hotter?
options: A has twice B’s absolute temperature.
Peak wavelength cannot relate to temperature.
B has twice A’s absolute temperature.
cpa.guide: The shorter peak wavelength indicates higher temperature; the ratio is 1.2/0.6 = 2.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Use λ_peak T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m·K. What is peak wavelength at 5,000 K?
cpa.guide: Divide the Wien constant by temperature: 2.9×10⁻³/5000 = 5.8×10⁻⁷ m.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A temperature is 727°C. Using T(K) ≈ T(°C) + 273, which temperature belongs in Wien’s law?
cpa.guide: Proportional temperature laws use absolute kelvin temperature.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A thermal spectrum peaks in the infrared. Which statement about the full spectrum is correct?
options: Its visible appearance must equal a single peak color.
It can still emit visible wavelengths; the peak is not its only emitted wavelength.
It emits exactly one infrared wavelength and nothing else.
cpa.guide: Thermal emission is broad; a peak marks a maximum, not an exclusive wavelength.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A distant hot object appears redder through a dusty path. Why is visible color alone an uncertain thermometer?
options: All red objects must have identical temperatures.
Wien’s law requires Celsius and so always fails.
Filtering, emission properties, and observation conditions can alter perceived color.
A spectrum contains no temperature information.
cpa.guide: Use the spectrum and model assumptions; apparent color can change without a temperature change.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.
